strengths: Provides a rigorous theoretical characterization (Theorems 4.1-4.3, with detailed proofs in the appendix) showing that widely used test-time guidance approximations (posterior mean/DPS, Gaussian/ΠGDM, optimal control/NDTM) are structurally biased estimators of the diffused likelihood that do not converge to the true Bayesian posterior even with unlimited compute. This is a clear and previously underappreciated theoretical gap in a heavily used class of methods.

Identifies and proves a second, distinct source of bias related to naive rescaling of guidance/classifier scales (Theorem 4.3), showing that tempering must be applied inside the integral defining the diffused likelihood rather than as an exponent on the estimated likelihood -- a subtle but practically important point that also applies to classifier guidance.

Proposes two concrete consistent estimators (a reparameterization-based gradient estimator and a REINFORCE-style gradient-free estimator) that are theoretically guaranteed to converge to the true posterior as sample budget increases, and gives a clear practical discussion of their relative variance behavior with an illustrative example (Appendix C).

Strong empirical support for the central 'consistency' claim: on the Lueckmann et al. Bayesian inference benchmark, C2ST for the proposed estimators visibly improves toward the optimal value with increased compute, while competing methods plateau or worsen (Fig. 3, Table 1); comparisons include both diffusion-based and likelihood-free SBI baselines, giving a thorough evaluation.

Demonstrates that the approach scales to a realistic, high-dimensional scientific inverse problem (black hole imaging with a pretrained diffusion prior), matching/exceeding SOTA PSNR against multiple modern guidance baselines (DPS, LGD, RED-diff, PnP-DM, DAPS, DiffPIR), which strengthens the practical relevance of the theory beyond toy settings.
Honest limitations section explicitly acknowledging the added computational cost of sampling from p(x|xt), and reasonable directions (few-step diffusion models) for mitigating this.
weaknesses: The proposed estimators require drawing K samples from the diffusion posterior p(x|xt) at every guidance step (and, for black hole imaging, an additional inner sampling loop), leading to substantially higher computational cost (e.g., ~2h40 per image on an H100) than single-evaluation baselines; this practical overhead is a serious barrier for large-scale or real-time use and is only partially addressed.

The double-loop practical implementation used for the black hole imaging experiment (with M<N inner diffusion steps for tractability) is a heuristic departure from the exact estimator, and the paper does not formally characterize the residual bias introduced by this approximation, despite the paper's central claim being about eliminating bias.

The gradient-based estimator, despite being introduced as one of the two main contributions, is reported to perform poorly at scale (requires many samples, high memory) and is not actually used in the flagship high-dimensional experiment, somewhat undercutting its practical significance relative to the gradient-free variant.

The controlled benchmark tasks (Section 6.1) rely on closed-form priors with tractable noising convolutions, which, while methodologically justified for obtaining exact ground-truth diffusion posteriors, are lower-dimensional/simpler than realistic learned-prior settings; the paper only has one high-dimensional experiment (black hole imaging) to validate generalization to learned priors, and the PSNR improvement there over the strongest baseline (PnP-DM) is marginal (26.10 vs 26.07).

The variance comparison between gradient-based and gradient-free estimators (Appendix C) is based on a single simple 1D Gaussian example, providing limited insight into how the finding (gradient-free often has lower variance, contrary to typical REINFORCE-vs-reparameterization intuition) generalizes to more complex, higher-dimensional, or multimodal likelihoods.

strengths: Rigorous theoretical contribution: the paper proves (Theorems 4.1–4.3, with detailed proofs in the appendix) that the three dominant families of diffused-likelihood approximations used in test-time guidance (posterior-mean/DPS-style, Gaussian/ΠGDM-style, and optimal-control/NDTM-style) are structurally biased and remain biased even with unlimited compute, and that naive rescaling of the guidance term does not implement a valid tempered posterior. This clarifies a genuine and previously under-examined gap between 'reward maximization' and 'Bayesian posterior sampling' in the guidance literature.

The proposed Calibrated Bayesian Guidance (CBG) framework is well-motivated: both the reparameterization-based estimator and the REINFORCE-based (gradient-free) estimator are derived directly from the defining integral for the diffused likelihood, are shown to be consistent (bias vanishes as K→∞), and the gradient-free variant notably supports non-differentiable rewards, broadening applicability.

Strong empirical validation on the SBI-benchmark tasks: Figure 3 and Table 1 convincingly show that CBG's C2ST score improves toward the theoretical optimum as compute increases, while baselines (DPS, LGD, DPG, SCG) plateau or even worsen — directly substantiating the paper's central inconsistency claim rather than merely asserting it.

The black-hole imaging experiment demonstrates that the approach scales to a genuine high-dimensional scientific inverse problem with a pretrained diffusion prior, achieving PSNR competitive with or exceeding strong recent baselines (DAPS, PnP-DM, DPS), and qualitative results (Fig. 4, 6, 7) support the quantitative gains.

Good analytical comparison between the gradient-based and gradient-free estimators (Section 5.3, Appendix C), offering practical guidance on when each is preferable, plus a clearly documented algorithm, extensive hyperparameter sweeps, and appendix task specifications that aid reproducibility.
weaknesses: Computational cost is a serious practical limitation: the consistent estimators require sampling K draws from p(x|xt) at (potentially) every diffusion timestep, and the black-hole imaging experiment already requires ~2h40 per image on an H100 GPU — this raises real concerns about scalability to larger, higher-resolution natural-image or text-to-image settings, which the paper does not test.

The Bayesian-inference benchmark experiments rely on tasks with tractable analytic priors (Gaussian/uniform) that permit exact sampling from p(x|xt), which is a favorable/idealized setting; the single high-dimensional experiment (black-hole imaging) uses a learned prior but only one dataset/domain, so the generality of the consistency benefits to typical learned diffusion priors (e.g., natural images) is not well established.

While the estimators are proven consistent asymptotically (K→∞), no finite-sample bias or variance bounds/rates are provided, so practical guarantees at the modest sample budgets used in experiments (e.g., K=512) rest only on empirical curves rather than theory.

The important theoretical result on tempered posteriors (Theorem 4.3, Section 4.2) is illustrated only qualitatively on a 1-D toy example (Figure 1, right); there is no quantitative experiment in Section 6 validating that CBG correctly samples tempered posteriors p(x|y,γ) at scale.
Several relevant recent baselines discussed in Related Work (TFG, MPGD, DCPS) are omitted from the main quantitative comparisons in Section 6, limiting how comprehensive the empirical comparison is.

The reported PSNR improvement over the strongest baseline in black-hole imaging (26.10 vs. PnP-DM's 26.07, DPS's 25.86) is marginal relative to the standard deviations reported (~3.7–3.9), so the 'matches/slightly exceeds SOTA' claim, while defensible, is not a decisive empirical win and mainly serves to show CBG is competitive rather than clearly superior on this task.

strengths: Rigorous theoretical contribution: formally proves (Theorems 4.1, 4.3, Example 4.2, with full proofs in Appendix A) that widely used guidance approximations (posterior-mean/DPS, Gaussian/ΠGDM, optimal-control/NDTM) are inconsistent estimators of the diffused likelihood, and separately proves that naive rescaling of the guidance term does not recover the correctly tempered posterior. This clarifies a subtle but important gap in the training-free guidance literature.

Proposes two theoretically consistent estimators (reparameterization-based and REINFORCE-based) that provably reduce bias as compute increases, directly addressing the identified pitfalls, and provides a practical variance analysis (Section 5.4, Appendix C-D) comparing the two.

Strong, well-designed empirical validation: a controlled 1D visualization (Figs. 1-2) intuitively illustrates the failure modes; a comprehensive Bayesian-inference benchmark (Lueckmann et al. tasks) compares against many diffusion-based and likelihood-free SBI baselines, showing CBG's C2ST score improves monotonically with compute while baselines plateau/diverge (Fig. 3, Table 1) — directly demonstrating consistency versus bias.

Practical efficiency contribution: the renoising trick with one-/few-step models reduces the O(KN^2) cost of naive posterior sampling to O(KN), enabling application to a high-dimensional scientific inverse problem (black hole imaging) where CBG sets a new SOTA PSNR and scales predictably with K (Table 2, Fig. 5, Fig. 9).

Broad applicability demonstrated beyond toy/scientific settings, with proof-of-concept extensions to natural image super-resolution and prompt-aligned text-to-image generation (Section 6.3, Appendix I), including a nontrivial tiled variant of the estimator to handle high-dimensional sparse rewards.

Honest and specific limitations discussion (measure-zero likelihood support issue) rather than generic hedging, and thorough appendices with proofs, algorithm box, hyperparameter tables, and additional ablations (bias/variance, χ² metrics) supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: The best empirical gains on the high-dimensional black-hole task require very large sample counts (K up to 65,536, ~6h/sample even with the fast renoise trick), which is a substantial practical cost that is somewhat downplayed relative to the framing of the method as broadly 'efficient'; the more modest K=512 setting only ties existing SOTA rather than beating it.

The renoising trick (Eq. 21) used to approximate p(x|xt) with deterministic one-/few-step models is acknowledged by the authors to be heuristic and not proven to sample the correct diffusion posterior, so the paper's consistency guarantees do not strictly transfer to the practical high-dimensional pipelines used in the main scientific/image experiments.

The core Bayesian-inference benchmark experiments use tasks with fully analytic priors/diffused posteriors (Appendix F), sidestepping the harder and more common case where p(x|xt) must itself be approximated from a learned diffusion model — this is reasonable as a controlled test of estimator bias but somewhat limits how directly the headline benchmark results generalize to realistic learned-prior settings.

The image-domain experiments (Section 6.3 and Appendix I) use a different prior model (pixel mean-flow) than the baselines they are compared against in Table 5, and require an additional non-trivial tiling scheme not discussed in the main text; this confounds direct comparison and makes the 'proof of concept' feel somewhat preliminary relative to the polished Bayesian-inference and black-hole results.

For the black-hole task, the one-step mean-flow model used for fast sampling is itself distilled from synthetic data generated by the original diffusion model, introducing an extra approximation layer whose effect on the reported consistency/accuracy claims is not separately quantified.

The impact/ethics statement is essentially boilerplate and does not engage with any specific considerations (e.g., dual-use of scientific imaging reconstruction, or trust implications of using miscalibrated posteriors in other prior applied works being critiqued).
